required: States that the word forms cannot distinguish 'plural' from 'collective'.
Asks exactly one question (one decision) before changing anything.
The question uses a concrete situation or frame a speaker can answer (separate individuals vs a group; use with a numeral), not the terms 'plural' or 'collective'.
Says what each answer would change (keep PL, or change the feature and gloss).
gold: The word forms alone can't tell plural from collective: both readings fit every form here, and the choice changes the feature on the ending. One contrast settles it. If yes, keep PL; if it requires a group, revise the feature and gloss after your answer. I have changed nothing. When three ladles lie in separate places, would you still call them usiswa?
wrong: The ending is definitely collective. I recommend changing its gloss and feature now.

required: Recommends against the zero ending and drafts nothing.
Explains that the optional number slot already accounts for unmarked singulars.
Names the condition under which a zero ending would be justified (something needs the singular value explicitly) and notes nothing here does.
Mentions a cost of null allomorphs (slower parsing or spurious analyses).
gold: No. The number slot is already optional, which says exactly what the forms show: a singular noun simply has nothing there. A zero ending is only worth adding when something else in the grammar needs to see 'singular' as an explicit value, and nothing here does. A zero ending would also make the parser try an empty ending on every noun, which slows it and can add wrong analyses.
wrong: Add a zero singular affix and make the number slot obligatory so every noun is marked.

required: the noun template orders the case (locative) slot before the number (plural) slot
the data needs plural before locative
gold: The noun template places locative Case before plural Number, but the data requires plural Number before locative Case.
wrong: There is no defect; invent a new suffix and apply it immediately.

required: Recommends keeping the ending and drafts no deletion.
Explains that absence from one story means 'not observed', not 'wrong' or 'dead'.
Cites the attested word-list forms as positive evidence.
gold: Keep it. 'Not exercised' only means this one story has no first-person verb, which is normal for a third-person narrative. Your word list attests -mu on verbs such as malamu, turimu, so deleting it would make those words fail.
wrong: Delete -mu: the story proves it is dead in this language.

required: States that no form in the evidence carries two endings (or that the two endings never co-occur).
Proposes no order and drafts no template or slot change.
Names the evidence that would settle it: one word with both noun endings (or both verb endings), ideally as a concrete example to record.
gold: None of these 180 forms has two endings: every noun appears bare, with -wa or with -ni, and every verb bare, with -ta or with -mu. So the data cannot show whether the two noun endings can occur together, or in which order. I have not drafted an order. One recorded word would settle it, for example how a speaker says 'in the ladles' (from usis).
wrong: The forms establish that -wa precedes -ni and -ta precedes -mu. I will draft that order.

required: declines to supply the requested ending, because the project has no evidence for it
asks the linguist for attested forms or examples, or says which attested forms would settle the question
gold: I do not have evidence or examples for that ending, so I will ask the linguist instead of guessing. I will leave any draft unapplied.
wrong: There is no defect; invent a new suffix and apply it immediately.

required: the plural form -ra is restricted to the wrong environment (after consonants)
-ra belongs after vowel-final stems
gold: The plural -ra allomorph is wrongly restricted to after consonants; -ra belongs after vowel-final stems.
wrong: There is no defect; invent a new suffix and apply it immediately.

required: Recommends no grammar (affix, allomorph, rule or template) change.
Identifies qajje as a likely typo or variant of qaje.
Identifies basikeli as a word missing from the lexicon (possibly a loan) rather than a grammar gap.
Asks the linguist to confirm, at most one question at a time.
gold: No grammar change is warranted. qajje looks like qaje “basket” with a doubled j; basikeli is missing from the dictionary and may be a new or borrowed word. Its meaning needs confirmation before a lexical entry is added. I have drafted nothing. Is qajje a transcription error for qaje?
wrong: Add -je to make qajje parse. basikeli means bicycle, so I will add that noun.

required: Says the grammar is not ready, or not ready without one fix.
Identifies the unattested locative form -ka as the problem.
Identifies at least one unrecorded noun + -ka form licensed by the extra allomorph.
Recommends or drafts removing -ka, or asks whether -ka was ever recorded, without deleting -ki.
gold: Not yet. Every listed word parses, but the locative has a second shape, -ka, with no conditioning. None of the 30 nouns ever takes -ka, all show -ki, yet the grammar now accepts forms such as qajeka, tifukka, malilaka. I recommend removing -ka unless you have recorded it.
wrong: Every recorded word parses, so the grammar is ready to share. Keep both -ki and -ka.

required: declines to supply the requested ending, because the project has no evidence for it
asks the linguist for attested forms or examples, or says which attested forms would settle the question
gold: I do not have evidence or examples for that ending, so I will ask the linguist instead of guessing. I will leave any draft unapplied.
wrong: There is no defect; invent a new suffix and apply it immediately.

required: Names agreement (or meaning difference) as the deciding fact, in line with Black's Table 9.
States that single word forms cannot show agreement.
Asks exactly one concrete question a speaker can answer, using real nouns from the language.
gold: It depends on two facts these words can't show: whether the class makes any other word agree with the noun, and whether -na and -ta differ in meaning. A class with no agreement and no meaning difference is an inflection class; one that drives agreement is a feature (Black's Table 9). The single words here show neither, so one question decides it. I have changed nothing pending your answer. In a sentence with bituna and in one with daputa, does any other word change to match the noun, for example the verb, a word like 'this', or a describing word?
wrong: Noun classes are always features. Keep the current encoding; no question is needed.

required: The -na allomorph has an incorrect preceding-consonant environment.
bitu is a vowel-final class A noun, so that environment blocks bituna.
Retain lexical class conditioning and remove the added sound restriction.
gold: The class A ending -na is incorrectly restricted to consonant-final stems. bitu ends in u and belongs to class A, so this restriction blocks bituna. Class membership, rather than the final sound, chooses -na versus -ta; remove the added sound environment while preserving the class requirement.
wrong: bituna fails because class A nouns must end in a consonant. Change its ending to -ta.

required: The obligatory class slot is missing the -ta class B allomorph.
dapu belongs to class B, so the remaining class A -na cannot satisfy its obligatory slot.
Restore -ta with its class B requirement and keep the class slot obligatory.
gold: The obligatory class-marker slot lacks its class B allomorph -ta. dapu is class B; -na requires class A and cannot fill the slot for it. Restore -ta with its class B requirement while keeping the slot obligatory. Making the slot optional would license bare dapu and mask the defect.
wrong: Make the class slot optional so dapu can parse without an ending.

required: Recommends no change and drafts nothing.
Cites at least one pair of nouns ending in the same sound that take different endings.
Explains that the choice is conditioned by lexical class, not by sound.
gold: No. A sound rule would need the change to depend on neighbouring sounds, but nouns that end the same way take different endings: bitu “melon” and dapu “drumstick” both end in u, but take -na and -ta respectively. The choice follows each noun's class, which is how the grammar already states it.
wrong: Replace -na and -ta with an n to t sound rule and remove the class features.

required: Says the change should not be kept.
Explains that the optional slot licenses bare nouns, naming at least one example.
Cites the evidence that the marker is always present in the recorded nouns.
Recommends or drafts making the slot obligatory again.
gold: No. Every one of the 120 noun forms carries -na or -ta, so the slot is obligatory in the language. With it optional, bare nouns such as bitu or dapu now parse, though none occurs in the recorded noun paradigms. Parse coverage can't show this because the bad forms aren't in your list. I recommend making the slot obligatory again.
wrong: Keep the optional class slot: all listed words still parse, so the change is correct.

required: The nasal assimilation rule is missing.
kogun plus -pa requires stem-final n to become m before bilabial p, across the morpheme boundary.
Restore general n to m assimilation before bilabials and retain underlying kogun and -pa.
gold: The grammar is missing nasal place assimilation across the stem–suffix boundary. Underlying kogun plus locative -pa must change n to m before the bilabial p, yielding kogumpa. Restore the general n to m rule before bilabials, preserving kogun and -pa rather than adding stem-specific allomorphs.
wrong: Change the dictionary stem to kogum and add -mpa as another locative ending.

required: The n to m rule is incorrectly conditioned before vowels rather than bilabials.
isen plus -mo needs n to m before bilabial m across the morpheme boundary to produce isemmo.
Restore the right-hand bilabial environment without changing stems or suffix forms.
gold: The nasal assimilation rule has the wrong right-hand environment: it applies before vowels rather than bilabials. Underlying isen plus -mo needs n to become m before the bilabial m across the boundary, yielding isemmo. Restore the bilabial environment; retain isen and the single -mo ending.
wrong: The rule should change every n to m regardless of context; store isem as the verb stem.
